units.text: Before the Prophet ﷺ Departed: Migrants Whose Journeys Were Not Alike
How did migrants precede the Prophet ﷺ to Medina, and what obstacles did some face on the road or in being separated from their families?

The migration was not a single caravan departing on one day. One report places Abu Salama among the earliest to head for Medina, while al-Bara’s report describes Mus‘ab ibn ‘Umayr and Ibn Umm Maktum as the first to reach his people. Behind the order of names lie different stories of departure: a family prevented from staying together, companions who did not all reach their meeting place, and a migrant who gave up his wealth to clear the way.
A Family Divided and Reunited

Ibn Ishaq places Abu Salama ‘Abd Allah ibn ‘Abd al-Asad among the first emigrants to Medina from the Quraysh clan of Banu Makhzum. He had returned from Abyssinia, suffered harm from Quraysh, and heard that some of the Ansar had embraced Islam; so he left for Medina.

Umm Salama relates that she mounted Abu Salama’s camel with their son Salama. Men of Banu al-Mughira stopped her from leaving and took her away; Banu ‘Abd al-Asad took the child, while Abu Salama went on to Medina. She says she would go out every morning to al-Abtah and weep, for a year or nearly that long.

Then she was permitted to join her husband and her son was returned to her. She set out with him; ‘Uthman ibn Talha met her at al-Tan‘im, led her camel, and helped her along the way. At Quba he pointed out the village where Abu Salama was staying, then returned to Mecca. In her account, what had proved impossible at the first departure was thus accomplished.
The Three Companions’ Rendezvous and What Happened to ‘Ayyash

‘Umar relates that he agreed with ‘Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi‘a and Hisham ibn al-‘As on a place to meet when they intended to migrate: if one was detained, the other two would proceed. ‘Umar and ‘Ayyash arrived; Hisham did not. The two then stayed among Banu ‘Amr ibn ‘Awf at Quba.

After their arrival, Abu Jahl and al-Harith ibn Hisham came to ‘Ayyash, telling him that his mother had vowed not to comb her hair or seek shade until she saw him. ‘Umar warned him and offered half his wealth if he would stay, then lent him his she-camel when he insisted on returning. Partway along the road they bound him and took him back to Mecca: reaching Medina had not ended the danger for ‘Ayyash.
Suhayb’s Wealth and an Open Road

In a report conveyed by Ibn Hisham from Abu ‘Uthman al-Nahdi, Suhayb wanted to migrate but some people prevented him from leaving with both himself and his wealth. He offered them his wealth in return for letting him go, and they accepted. When the news reached the Prophet ﷺ, he said, according to this report: “Suhayb has profited, Suhayb has profited.”
Accounts of Arrival

Al-Bara says in al-Bukhari’s report: “The first to come to us were Mus‘ab ibn ‘Umayr and Ibn Umm Maktum.” Another route names those who came after them and then mentions ‘Umar with twenty people before the Prophet ﷺ arrived. People arrived in succession; they did not all leave with the Prophet ﷺ.

In Ibn ‘Umar’s report cited by al-Bayhaqi, those arriving from Mecca settled at a place he called al-‘Usba, among them ‘Umar, Abu ‘Ubayda, and Salim, the freedman of Abu Hudhayfa. Salim led them in prayer because he knew the most Qur’an. Ibn Sa‘d’s account describes him leading the emigrants at Quba before the Prophet ﷺ arrived.
What Kind of “First” Do We Mean?

Ibn Isḥāq names Abū Salama as the first emigrant to Medina from the Quraysh of Banū Makhzūm and places his departure a year before the pledge of the people of al-ʿAqaba. Ibn Kathīr transmits another formulation from him: Abū Salama had intended to return to Abyssinia before turning toward Medina. Al-Barāʾ names Muṣʿab and Ibn Umm Maktūm as “the first to come to us”; his “to us” refers to those who arrived among his people.

In Mūsā ibn ʿUqba’s account from al-Zuhrī, people left in successive groups. The report names Umm Salama as the first woman to arrive in a camel litter; some named Umm ʿAbd Allāh bint Abī Ḥathma instead, and the report adds “God knows best”. Ibn Isḥāq names ʿĀmir’s wife as Laylā bint Abī Ḥathma. Umm Salama recounts that her departure with Abū Salama was interrupted when his family and hers separated her from her son and husband.
Umm Salama’s separation and journey to Quba
Umm Salama estimated her separation from her husband and son at “a year or nearly that long”. She says ʿUthmān ibn Ṭalḥa helped her on the road until she reached Quba.

ʿUmar relates what happened to ʿAyyāsh; Ibn Isḥāq reports that he was displayed bound before the people of Mecca on the authority of an unnamed member of ʿAyyāsh’s family. Ibn Hishām’s account of Suhayb is an indirect report from Abū ʿUthmān al-Nahdī, not Suhayb’s direct testimony.
Suhayb and Salim: differing details in the reports

Another account of Suhayb transmitted by Ibn Kathīr from al-Bayhaqī says he had intended to leave with the Prophet ﷺ and Abū Bakr, but young men stopped him. He offered measures of gold and pointed out two garments, then reached the Prophet ﷺ at Quba. In Abū ʿUthmān’s indirect report he gives up his wealth, without mention of those measures or garments. The wording “the transaction profited” in this route differs from “Suhayb profited” in the indirect report.
Al-Bayhaqī’s account of ʿUmar also passes through Ibn Isḥāq, from Nāfiʿ, from Ibn ʿUmar. The spelling of the rendezvous word and some vocalization of the place name differ from Ibn Hishām’s version.

Ibn Kathīr transmits from Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān an account of Sālim leading prayer at al-ʿUṣba; its chain has wording that differs from al-Bayhaqī’s. Ibn Saʿd names Quba as the place where Sālim led the emigrants in prayer before the Prophet ﷺ arrived. The account of Ibn ʿUmar instead names al-ʿUṣba.

What happened to Abu Salama’s family when they first tried to leave?
Banu al-Mughira took the mother, Banu ‘Abd al-Asad took the child, and Abu Salama went on.
According to Umm Salama’s testimony in Ibn Ishaq’s account.
They all traveled on a single camel as far as Quba.
In Umm Salama’s testimony, the family was separated when their relatives stopped them.
Abu Salama went on; Umm Salama was detained, and Abu Salama’s relatives took her son.
Correct: the husband left, and the mother was separated from her son.
Umm Salama left first with the child, while Abu Salama remained in Mecca.
Umm Salama relates that Abu Salama was the one who went on to Medina first.
How did Umm Salama and her son reach Abu Salama after their separation?
The account of her departure with her son goes on to describe ‘Uthman helping her and their arrival at Quba.
Read the two consecutive portions of Umm Salama’s account together.
‘Umar accompanied them from his meeting place with ‘Ayyash to Quba.
The story of ‘Umar and ‘Ayyash is a separate account, not an account of Umm Salama’s escort.
Her son was returned to her; then ‘Uthman ibn Talha helped her on the road and pointed out where her husband was staying in Quba.
Correct: she relates that she departed with her son after he was returned to her, and ‘Uthman accompanied her.
She left with her husband at the outset and was never separated from him.
Umm Salama relates that she was separated from her husband and son before she rejoined him.
How did Umm Salama qualify the length of time she wept at al-Abtah?
In the reading Umm Salama says, “a year or nearly that long.”
These are her reported words, not an independent calendrical calculation.
Exactly one full year, ending on a known day.
The text says a year or nearly that long, without naming a particular day.
A year or nearly that long.
Correct: the phrase is approximate, not a date with a day and month.
Only three nights.
That is not how Umm Salama describes the length of their separation.
How does Ibn Ishaq’s account of Abu Salama differ from al-Bara’s wording, ‘the first to come to us’?
Ibn Ishaq qualified his description of Abu Salama, and al-Bara specified the recipients by saying “to us.”
The comparison does not settle every question about the order of arrivals.
Discard one text, because both refer without qualification to all emigrants.
Each text has its own qualification: Ibn Ishaq’s wording and al-Bara’s audience.
Keep Abu Salama’s precedence within Ibn Ishaq’s qualification and understand “to us” in al-Bara’s words from the perspective of those addressed.
Correct: the different perspectives do not license applying either statement to everyone.
We conclude that Abu Salama and Mus‘ab arrived together on the same day.
Neither text gives a single shared date of arrival.
Which wording preserves the variation in the account of the first woman in a litter alongside Umm Salama’s account of separation?
Musa’s route says “some people say” and then “God knows best”; Umm Salama’s testimony describes her separation from her husband.
The question concerns these two accounts, not a general ruling on the first woman to migrate.
The two texts establish that Umm Salama accompanied Abu Salama all the way to Medina when he first left.
Umm Salama’s account describes their separation at the outset.
Musa’s route names Umm Salama and also reports a view naming Umm ‘Abd Allah; this list does not imply that Umm Salama traveled on the day her husband left.
Correct: the account itself includes both views and ends with a reservation.
No source names any woman among the earliest arrivals.
The account names Umm Salama and Umm ‘Abd Allah; Ibn Ishaq also describes Layla bint Abi Hathma.
According to ‘Umar’s account, who arrived at the rendezvous and what had the three agreed?
‘Umar relates that they would regard anyone not there in the morning as detained, and the other two would go on.
According to Ibn Ishaq’s route through Nafi‘, Ibn ‘Umar, and ‘Umar.
‘Umar, ‘Ayyash and Hisham all arrived and waited for anyone missing.
The account says Hisham did not arrive and the others were to proceed.
‘Umar and ‘Ayyash arrived and proceeded as the three had agreed if one of them was detained.
Correct: Hisham was detained, and his companions did not wait for him.
Only ‘Ayyash arrived; he did not proceed until everyone had gathered.
‘Umar arrived with him, and they proceeded after Hisham was detained.
What did ‘Umar offer ‘Ayyash when he wanted to return with Abu Jahl and al-Harith?
‘Umar warned ‘Ayyash and offered him half his wealth and then his she-camel, but ‘Ayyash left with the two men.
‘Umar’s report here is distinct from the addition attributed to some of ‘Ayyash’s family about displaying him bound.
Half his wealth if he would stay, then his she-camel when he insisted on returning.
Correct: the warning and offer preceded his being taken in bonds.
Measures of gold and two garments so he could travel freely.
Those details belong to the other route about Suhayb, not to ‘Ayyash’s account.
He gave him no advice and offered him nothing.
‘Umar relates that he advised him and then offered the wealth and the she-camel.
To whom is the addition about displaying ‘Ayyash bound before the people of Mecca attributed?
Ibn Ishaq resumes the account of this display by saying that one of ‘Ayyash’s family told him of it.
The question concerns only the voice behind this addition.
To ‘Umar in the same directly transmitted statement.
The addition begins with a new link of transmission from some of ‘Ayyash’s family.
To unnamed members of ‘Ayyash’s family in Ibn Ishaq’s transmission.
Correct: the text separates the addition from ‘Ayyash’s family from ‘Umar’s words.
To Suhayb in Abu ‘Uthman’s report.
Abu ‘Uthman’s report concerns Suhayb, not ‘Ayyash.
What did Suhayb offer in Abu ‘Uthman’s report in Ibn Hisham, without importing details from the other route?
Abu ‘Uthman’s report says he gave them his wealth; the measures of gold and two garments occur in the route about Suhayb quoted by Ibn Kathir.
The report is introduced with “it was mentioned to me” and “it reached me.”
His wealth in return for their letting him go.
Correct: the report mentions his wealth without specifying measures of gold or the two garments.
‘Umar’s she-camel so that he could return to Mecca.
The she-camel belongs to ‘Ayyash’s account, not the report about Suhayb.
Measures of gold and two garments.
The gold and garments occur in the route cited by Ibn Kathir, not in Abu ‘Uthman’s report in Ibn Hisham.
Why did Salim lead the group in prayer in Ibn ‘Umar’s account in al-Bayhaqi?
Ibn ‘Umar links Salim’s leading the prayer to his knowing more Qur’an than the others.
The report calls their stopping place al-‘Usba.
Because he was the oldest.
The account does not give age as the reason.
Because he owned the house in which they stayed.
The account does not say he was their host.
Because he knew the most Qur’an.
Correct: that is the reason given in Ibn ‘Umar’s text.
Which place is named in Ibn Umar’s report as transmitted by al-Bayhaqi, and which place is named in the continuation by Ibn Sa‘d?
Each report describes the location in its own words; mentioning Quba does not prove that the name al-‘Usba refers to it in every route.
This compares the two readings; it is not an independent geographical investigation.
Both texts name only al-‘Usba and give the same list of people.
Al-Bayhaqi names al-‘Usba and Ibn Sa‘d names Quba; their lists are not worded identically.
Ibn ‘Umar’s report names al-‘Usba, and Ibn Sa‘d’s continuation mentions Quba; the wording alone does not establish that the two places are identical.
Correct: retain each report’s qualification of the location.
Neither names a location.
One says al-‘Usba and the other says Quba.
This chapter’s placement before the chapter on al-‘Aqaba is a reading order, not a claim that every reported event concerning these migrants preceded every pledge or that they all left at once.
The chapter readings do not resolve the disagreement about the first woman in a litter or date the day of separation or reunion; the interval in Umm Salama’s account is a year or nearly that long.

When Abu Salama resolved to leave for Medina, he saddled his camel for me, placed me on it, and placed my son Salama ibn Abi Salama in my lap. He then led the camel with me on it. When men of Banu al-Mughira ibn ‘Abd Allah ibn ‘Umar ibn Makhzum saw him, they confronted him and said, “As for yourself, you have prevailed over us in that; but what about this wife of yours? Why should we let you take her about the land?” They pulled the camel’s halter from his hand and took me away from him. Banu ‘Abd al-Asad, Abu Salama’s kin, grew angry and said, “By God, we will not leave our son with her when you have taken her from our kinsman.” They tugged my son Salama between them until they dislocated his arm; Banu ‘Abd al-Asad took him away, Banu al-Mughira detained me, and my husband Abu Salama went on to Medina. Thus my husband, my son, and I were separated. Every morning I would go and sit at al-Abtah and keep weeping until a year, or nearly that long, had passed. Then a man of my paternal kin, one of Banu al-Mughira, passed by and saw my condition. He took pity on me and said to Banu al-Mughira, “Will you not let this poor woman go? You have separated her from her husband and child!” They said to me, “Join your husband if you wish.” Banu ‘Abd al-Asad then returned my son to me. I saddled my camel, took my son and set him in my lap, and left intending to reach my husband in Medina. I had no one else with me. I thought, “I will manage with the help of whomever I meet until I reach my husband.” At al-Tan‘im I met ‘Uthman ibn Talha ibn Abi Talha, of Banu ‘Abd al-Dar. He said, “Where are you going, daughter of Abu Umayya?” I replied, “I am going to my husband in Medina.” “Do you have no one with you?” he asked. “No, by God, except God and this little son of mine,” I said. He said, “By God, you cannot be left on your own.” He took the camel’s halter and went along with me, leading it. By God, I have never traveled with an Arab man whom I considered more honorable than he. When we reached a stopping place, he made the camel kneel for me and moved away. Once I had dismounted he took my camel aside, unloaded it, and tied it to a tree, then withdrew

[away from me] to a tree and lay beneath it. As departure time approached he came to my camel, brought it over and saddled it. Then he moved away and said, “Mount.” Once I had mounted and was settled on the camel, he came, took its halter, and led it until he brought me to the next stopping place. He continued to do this until he brought me to Medina. When he saw the village of Banu ‘Amr ibn ‘Awf at Quba, he said, “Your husband is in this village”—Abu Salama was staying there—“so enter it with God’s blessing.” Then he turned back to Mecca.

of God ﷺ for Medina were Abu Salama ibn ‘Abd al-Asad and his wife Umm Salama bint Abi Umayya; ‘Amir ibn Rabi‘a and his wife Umm ‘Abd Allah bint Abi Hathma. It is said that the first woman in a litter to reach Medina was Umm Salama; some people say it was Umm ‘Abd Allah—and God knows best. Also Mus‘ab ibn ‘Umayr, ‘Uthman ibn Maz‘un, Abu Hudhayfa ibn ‘Utba ibn Rabi‘a, ‘Abd Allah ibn Jahsh, ‘Uthman ibn al-Sharid, and ‘Ammar ibn Yasir. Abu Salama and ‘Abd Allah ibn Jahsh stayed among Banu ‘Amr ibn ‘Awf. Then ‘Umar ibn al-Khattab and ‘Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi‘a left with some companions and stayed among Banu ‘Amr ibn ‘Awf. Then came the search involving Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, al-Harith ibn Hisham, al-‘As ibn Hisham, and ‘Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi‘a, their maternal brother. The two said: When the seventy departed from the Messenger of God ﷺ, he was reassured, for God had granted him protectors, a people capable of war, with resources and courage. The polytheists intensified their persecution of the Muslims on learning of their departure; they constrained his companions, harassed them, and inflicted insults and harm upon them beyond what they had done before. The Messenger of God’s companions ﷺ complained of this to him and sought his permission to migrate. He said, “I was shown the place of your migration: I was shown a palm-bearing salt flat between two lava fields. If al-Sarat had been a land of palms and salt flats, I would have said it was that place.” He remained for some days; then he came out to his companions joyful and said, “I have been informed of the place of your migration: it is Yathrib. Whoever wants to depart, let him go there.” The people began preparing, making arrangements with one another, supporting one another, and departing in secret. The first of the Messenger of God’s companions ﷺ to arrive in Medina was Abu Salama ibn ‘Abd al-Asad. After him came ‘Amir ibn Rabi‘a with his wife Layla bint Abi Hathma; she was the first woman in a litter

to reach Medina. Then the Messenger of God’s companions ﷺ came in successive groups, staying with the Ansar in their homes. The Ansar sheltered, supported, and shared their means with them. Salim, the freedman of Abu Hudhayfa, led the emigrants in prayer at Quba before the Messenger of God ﷺ arrived. When the Muslims left in their migration to Medina, Quraysh grew fiercely hostile toward them, became embittered and angry at those of their young men who departed. Some of the Ansar had pledged to the Messenger of God ﷺ at the later al-‘Aqaba, then returned to Medina. When the first emigrants arrived at Quba, these men went out to the Messenger of God ﷺ in Mecca and returned with his companions in the migration; they were thus Ansar who also emigrated. They were Dhakwan ibn ‘Abd Qays, ‘Uqba ibn Wahb ibn Kalada, al-‘Abbas ibn ‘Ubada ibn Nadla, and Ziyad ibn Labid. All the Muslims left for Medina, and none remained in Mecca except the Messenger of God ﷺ, Abu Bakr, ‘Ali, someone subjected to trial and detained, someone ill, or someone too weak to leave.
What Was the Hijrah—and Why Did Muslims Leave Makkah?

The Hijrah was the migration of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and his followers from Makkah to Medina. Some Muslims faced opposition and harm in Makkah. In Medina, people had already embraced Islam, giving those who left Makkah a community of fellow believers to join.

Some of the Prophet’s companions went ahead of him to Medina. Their journeys were not easy: some were separated from their families, one was brought back bound, and one gave up his wealth so that he could go on his way.
